Items.Authors: Félix Gudin, Nicolas Forget
Items.Title: Swept-source heterodyne detection for interferometry in the H band
Items.Abstract: It is well established that direct-detection interferometry outperforms heterodyne interferometry in terms of signal-to-noise ratio at optical wavelengths, not only because of the limited electronic bandwidth of photodetectors (typically <100 GHz), but also due to the shot-noise contribution of the optical local oscillator. The large-scale production of high-quality and cost-effective telecom components in the J+H band, and more recently in the K band, may open new schemes for the heterodyne signal detection and processing (e.g. correlation) as well as for the transport, distribution and control of the local oscillator. We describe how high-repetition-rate frequency-swept sources and telecom components could be exploited to parallelize, at reasonable cost, a large number of coherent detectors to expand the spectral coverage. We also present a first laboratory single-channel proof of concept that achieves a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) probably sufficient for observing the brightest star

Items.Authors: A. C. Ruggeri, F. Schillirò, C. Trigilio, G. Nicotra, S. Buttaccio, S. Loru, M. G. Labate, G. Umana, P. R. Platania, C. Nocita
Items.Title: Technical upgrades for the Noto radio telescope for multimessenger perspectives in synergy with the KM3NeT
Items.Abstract: High-energy (HE) neutrinos are produced in energetic astrophysical phenomena, but identifying their sources remains challenging because of the limited angular resolution of current neutrino telescopes. Electromagnetic counterpart searches are therefore essential to localise the emitters and study the conditions leading to neutrino production. We present a "Next Generation EU -- KM3NeT4RR" project, aimed at monitoring potential HE-neutrino radio sources with the Noto radio telescope (NT) (INAF), building a long-term database of high-frequency radio behaviour and searching for correlations with KM3NeT events. The NT is being upgraded to extend its observing capabilities and improve data acquisition: the primary reflector has been refurbished, a new subreflector installed, and a tri-band receiver will observe simultaneously in the K, Q, and W bands. A dedicated down-converter has been designed and installed to interface the receiver with the SKARAB back-end for total-power observations.

Items.Authors: Mona El Morsy, Thayne Currie, Brianna Lacy, Danielle Bovie
Items.Title: Technology and science advancing observations with Roman coronagraph informed by ground-based high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: The Roman Coronagraph technology demonstration focuses on achieving <1e-7 contrasts within the instrument's dark hole and our ability to detect and characterize properties of faint companions around bright stars. In this talk, I describe results from a study of potential Roman Coronagraph technology demonstration phase observations focused on these goals, informed by the ongoing OASIS survey at the Subaru Telescope. OASIS provides at least three compelling targets for the technology demonstration phase: HIP 71618 B for the core contrast goal, HIP 54515 b for characterizing the system's performance, and HIP 99770 b for atmospheric characterization.

Items.Authors: Christopher Zamorano, Pedro Escarate
Items.Title: Telemetry-based methodology for identifying wind-induced torque in the elevation axis of an ALMA 12m total power antenna
Items.Abstract: The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), on the Chajnantor plateau (~5050 m a.s.l.), operates under persistent winds that can push its direct-drive actuators close to their current limits. This work presents a telemetry-driven, controller-agnostic method to estimate the motor current required at a target elevation θ* for a given wind speed v and direction ϕ. In the push–pull architecture, the differential current acts as a virtual torque sensor, Tnet = Kt (i1 − i2). Using static-hold segments (θ̇ ≈ 0), we fit an ordinary-least-squares model with (v cosϕ, v sinϕ) and elevation as predictors, achieving R² ≈ 0.95 over ~1.2×10⁴ samples (up to 13 m/s, 5°–88°). The identified map produces per-motor current forecasts and a current-margin indicator referenced to hardware limits, and is directly applicable to other telescopes using push–pull PMSM/PMLSM actuators.

Items.Authors: Bruno Quint, Tiago Ribeiro, Erik Dennihy, Brian Stalder, David Sanmatim, Keith Bechtol
Items.Title: Test management and coordination during the Vera C. Rubin Observatory commissioning and early operations using Zephyr Scale
Items.Abstract: The commissioning of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory required coordinating hundreds of integration and on-sky tests. To support this coordination, we adopted Zephyr Scale, a Jira-native test management tool, for system verification and high-level commissioning. We describe the workflow for creating, reviewing, and deploying stable Test Cases into daily Test Cycles. We present how we serialize complex steps within a test case into JSON files that interface with the observatory's real-time observation optimization engine, the Scheduler. Finally, we summarize the benefits and limitations of using Zephyr Scale, designed initially to coordinate software testing, for large-scale observatory commissioning and early operations.

Items.Authors: Congcong Zhang, Lixin Zheng, Lurun Shen, Dan Zhou, Fabo Feng, Yicheng Rui, Zhendong Chen, Jianjun Cao, Qi Wang, Yuanyuan Ding, Xinyang Chen, Qi Shao
Items.Title: The 10 square degree telescope for Tianyu project
Items.Abstract: The Tianyu Telescope is a 1-meter horizontal telescope mainly used for exoplanet exploration, including the transit signals of long-period exoplanets such as Jupiter and Neptune, and is used in conjunction with the JUST Telescope for exoplanet and time-domain scientific research.   The Tianyu Telescope, as a wide field of view main focus telescope, has a field of view of approximately 10 square degrees. Installing an 8k * 8k backlit high frame rate CMOS camera in the main focus can achieve high-frequency high-precision photometric sky survey with sub second sampling intervals. On the one hand, Jupiter like transit signals will be detected; On the other hand, a large number of high-energy transient sources, including supernovae, as well as short period variable stars, will also be discovered.

Items.Authors: Benjamin L. Schmitt
Items.Title: The Advanced Simons Observatory Energy Security Initiative: Enabling an Energy Secure Future for Remote Astronomical Telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO) is operating with an array of large- and small-aperture, millimeter-wavelength sensitive telescopes, making observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) at a high-altitude site on Cerro Toco in the Atacama Desert of Northern Chile. As SO begins primary CMB science objectives, a new science infrastructure initiative - the Advanced Simons Observatory (ASO) – has prioritized the design, integration, and operation of a new energy security facility, the core of which is a large-scale, high-altitude photovoltaic array (PVA) power plant (currently planned to be over 1 MW nameplate capacity with room for expansion up to 3 MW). The ASO PVA will ensure the long term energy security of SO site operations. This talk will describe the design, deployment, and early commissioning results of the ASO PVA, which is currently in the final stages of construction in Chile, and aims to have first light by Spring 2026, with transfer to nominal operations in mid-2026.

Items.Authors: Chiara Selmi, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Marco M. Riva, Alessio Zanutta, Matteo Genoni, Andrea Balestra, Nils Fisher, Matteo De Magistris
Items.Title: The AstroMBSE methodology: a comprehensive MBSE methodology to drive and support the development of future astronomical instruments
Items.Abstract: The AstroMBSE methodology addresses all the main systems engineering tasks that are usually encountered while developing astronomical instruments. The methodology addresses six main classical systems engineering topics, employing MBSE to make thier management more efficient and reliable. These topics are:  1. Design methodology  2. Requirements management  3. Interfaces management  4. Documentation management  5. Physical Structure management  6. Collaborative Systems Engineering  All these topics are designed to operate and work together to produce a synchronized and comprehensive representation of an astronomical instrument, based on a tailored versione of SysML V1 language, prepared to address the specifical context of astronomical instruments.  This methodology has been applied (at least partially) to some crucial future astronomical instruments like MORFEO and ANDES for ELT, and CUBES for VLT

Items.Authors: Maria Begoña García-Lorenzo, Jesús Aceituno, José Acosta Pulido, Romano Corradi, Pablo de Vicente, Francisco J. Herrada, Martín Guerrero, Antonio Marín-Franch, Miguel Sánchez-Portal, Olga Zamora
Items.Title: The Astronomy Infrastructure Network in Spain (RIA): promoting synergies, collaboration, and knowledge exchange in a multiwavelength and scientifically diverse landscape
Items.Abstract: The Astronomy Infrastructure Network (RIA) coordinates Spain’s major astronomical ICTS and the international facilities in which the country participates. Its mission is to promote collaboration, improve scientific and technological performance, and advise national institutions on current and future astronomical infrastructures and instrumentation. RIA spans optical, infrared, radio, high-energy, and solar facilities, enabling synergy groups that address shared operational and technical challenges and exchange practical solutions. Their work covers engineering and operations, instrumentation and detectors, data and digital infrastructures, AI, cybersecurity, communications, atmospheric monitoring, observational support, and sky-protection and sustainability strategies. RIA also organizes meetings to strengthen communication and showcase facilities. This contribution outlines RIA’s multi-wavelength ICTS, its coordination mechanisms, and its main recent achievements.

Items.Authors: Siqi Wang, Xiaoyan Li, Yiming Zhang, Ali Esamdin
Items.Title: The auto-guiding system of the Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto)
Items.Abstract: This paper introduces the offset auto-guiding system developed for the Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto) of Yunnan University. The system includes a statistical analysis of the acquisition probability of candidate stars within the guide field under different integration times, image preprocessing algorithms designed to correct for overscan, non-uniform dark-current response, non-uniform pixel response and field illumination, as well as bad columns and defective pixels, a stellar centroid extraction algorithm suitable for wide-field images containing multiple stars, and an automatic guide star selection algorithm for determining the optimal guiding target. The performance of the system was verified through on-sky observations. The test results show that, as the guide star integration time increased from 2 s to 30 s, the root-mean-square (RMS) centroid variation between consecutive frames decreased from 0.335″ and 0.360″ to 0.124″ and 0.116″ in the X and Y directions,

Items.Authors: Simone Iovenitti, Pietro Bruno, Giorgia Sironi, Gino Tosti, Michela Uslenghi, Stefano Germani, Mauro Fiorini, Salvatore Scuderi
Items.Title: The automatic mirror alignment system of ASTRI Mini-Array telescopes
Items.Abstract: In this contribution we address the challenge of mirror alignment for dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes used in both the ASTRI and CTAO-SST arrays. These instruments adopt a Schwarzschild–Couder optical design with a segmented 18-facet aspheric primary mirror and an extremely fast focal ratio (f/0.5). The alignment procedure must achieve high precision, while remaining fast and automated, given the large number of telescopes to calibrate. Hence, we developed the Mirror Alignment System (MAS), a software component implementing the operational logic and controlling hardware subsystems, such as mirror actuators and the optical camera. Through a closed-loop process based on successive approximations, MAS delivers the required positioning accuracy efficiently and autonomously. MAS is deployed during the Assembly, Integration, and Verification phase and operated through the engineering GUI. In July 2025 it was validated on-sky on ASTRI-2, achieving a PSF within requirements in ~two hours.

Items.Authors: Christian Eredia, Vincenzo Cianniello, Liana De Filippis, Enrico Cascone
Items.Title: The concurrent design strategy for astronomical instrumentation: first outcomes and future developments
Items.Abstract: The concurrent design methodology has been successfully implemented in many fields, especially for space applications. The possibility of implementing a similar strategy to the development of ground-based astronomical instrumentation is extremely promising, as it can help solve many of the issues in terms of efficiency and development time.  With this in mind, an effort has been made to tailor this approach to the peculiarities of the ground based astronomical applications being developed in the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics. With the main Concurrent Design Facility in Naples becoming operational at the beginning of 2026, the activities are now entering their most crucial phase, with dedicated sessions to case studies, in order to test and improve the proposed methodology.  This paper describes the first outcomes of these efforts and the next steps towards the establishment of concurrent design as a new paradigm for the design of astronomical instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Nanfei Yan, Qianhan Zhou, Jianhui Zhang, Ling Wei, Linhai Huang, Xuejun Rao, Lanqiang Zhang, Changhui Rao
Items.Title: The CPU-GPU based heterogeneous real-time controller for solar AO systems at 1-meter and 2.5-meter solar telescopes
Items.Abstract: To tackle high computational loads in solar adaptive optics, we developed a scalable CPU-GPU heterogeneous real-time controller (RTC). This architecture serves both the 1-meter NVST and 2.5-meter WeHoST telescopes. It employs a flexible task-parallelization strategy to dynamically distribute workloads between CPUs and GPUs based on system scale, minimizing latency. The paper details its application in both systems, presents achieved latency performance, and reports on-sky results from the NVST GLAO system alongside laboratory closed-loop results from the WeHoST testbed.

Items.Authors: A. B. Flood, C. O'Sullivan, M. L. Gradziel, D. Gayer, S. Marwede, C. G. Scóccola, E. S. Battistelli, P. de Bernardis, F. Columbro, A. Coppolecchia, B. Costanza, S. Ferazzoli, B. Garcia, M. Gervasi, A. Huchet, T. Laclavere, S. Masi, A. Mennella, N. Mirón-Granese, A. Paiella, M. Piat, E. Rasztocky, M. Regnier, G. E. Romero, S. A. Torchinsky, M. Zannoni
Items.Title: The effect of QUBIC beam uncertainty on the reconstruction of the CMB B-mode power spectrum
Items.Abstract: The Q and U Bolometric Interferometer for Cosmology (QUBIC) is a telescope which will observe the cosmic microwave background with the goal of detecting primordial B-modes. In QUBIC, a cold reflective optical combiner superimposes the re-emitted beams from an array of aperture feedhorns onto transition edge sensors, a type of superconducting bolometer. It has a complex multi-peaked synthesised beam which we model with physical optics. This novel design allows QUBIC to have precise control over instrument systematics and to remove signals from astronomical foregrounds, which would otherwise obscure the polarisation.   This work investigates how uncertainties in the beam pattern affect the observations made by QUBIC, and to what precision the beam must be known to measure the B-modes to a given accuracy. We use beam simulations and QUBIC’s data-reduction pipeline to show the effects of aberrations and uncertainty in the beam on the reconstruction of the B-mode power spectrum.

Items.Authors: Alexander Fitzner, Emanuel Kopp, Karsten Westerdorff, Carlos Arcos Carrasco, Olaf Hillenmeier, Stefan Weisse, Alexander Wirth, Johannes Buschek, Martin Pertenaïs, Till Hagelschuer, Yaquelin Miriam M. Rosas-Ortiz, Ingo Walter, Gabriel J. Schwarzkopf, Thomas Säuberlich, Patrick Dern, Simone del Togno, Andreas Pohl, Dennis Wendler, Belinda Wendler, Bernd Ulmer, Horst-Georg Lötzke, Nils Mueller, Ana-Catalina Plesa, Giulia Alemanno, Gisbert Peter
Items.Title: The electrical design and development of the Venus Emissivity Mapper (VEM) for VERITAS and EnVision
Items.Abstract: The Venus Emissivity Mapper (VEM) is an IR-spectrometer designed to measure surface thermal radiation. The VEM’s electrical design is tailored to meet the unique requirements of two distinct missions: NASA/JPL’s VERITAS and ESA’s EnVision. The VEM must accommodate varying interface and environmental demands while maintaining high performance and reliability. This dual-mission approach presents significant challenges, including differing power, data handling interfaces, and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) environments. This paper discusses the differences between the two instrument variants in terms of interfaces and environmental constraints, provides an overview of the general electronics architecture, and highlights mission-specific adaptations. It further details the key challenges encountered during early development—particularly concerning the detector, FPGA and replacement of the hybrid DC-DC converter—before presenting the results of functional and performance tests.

Items.Authors: Remko Stuik, Yu Chieh Huang, Gilles Otten, Dirk Lesman, Ioannis Politopoulos, Chad Salo, Emilie Bouzerand, Adrian M. Glauser, Sander Kwast, Dennis Dolkens, Roy van Boekel, Wolfgang Brandner, Ioannis Argyriou, Gert Raskin, Wim De Meester, Jeffrey Lynn, Bernhard R. Brandl, Felix C. M. Bettonvil
Items.Title: The first steps of system level integration of METIS: from facility to cryostat
Items.Abstract: METIS, the Mid-Infrared ELT Imager and Spectrometer, has now fully entered its system integration phase. Over the last few years, the preparations were made, both for the system-level integration hall, as well as in the integration and verification of the various METIS subsystems. Late 2025, the cryostat was the first subsystem delivered to the system-level facility and was integrated with the control system. As further subsystems are integrated, validated, and as each individual subsystem passes its verification tests, they are added, completing the full METIS system.    In this paper, we describe the facility, the workflow, and how METIS is verified, using the first subsystems as a pathfinder towards the full integration. We describe some of the results of the first system-level verifications, as well as how the initial integration and verification plans have met with reality, and how this impacts the further integration, towards a fully operational METIS.

Items.Authors: Colby A. Jurgenson, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Mark Mueller, William Podgorski, Sagi Ben-Ami, Flavio Cruz, Henrique Lupinari, Marlon Correia, Tomas Andrade, Shiang-Yu Wang, TzuLing Chen, Chun-Yen Wen, Matthew Leung
Items.Title: The G-CLEF advanced wavelength calibration system architecture and design
Items.Abstract: The GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) is a designed fiber-fed, optical echelle spectrograph (350 to 950 nm) that is to be a first light instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). G-CLEF will have four resolution modes (23k > R < 110k) with a precision radial velocity (PRV) goal of 10 cm/sec in the highest resolution mode. A dichroic in the G-CLEF spectrograph optical train separates light into a blue (350 to 540 nm) and a red (540 to 950 nm) channel, each with its own camera optics and detector. This paper will provide an overview of the Advanced Wavelength Calibration System (AWCS) architecture and design. The AWCS will consist of two stabilized Fabry-Perot etalons (one for the blue channel and one for the red), a laser frequency comb, and the optomechanical infrastructure and fiber feed system to deliver three calibration modes to the spectrograph: 1) LFC stand-alone, 2) etalon stand-alone, and 3) simultaneous LFC + etalon. The etalons will provide the main source fo

Items.Authors: Martin J. Dyer, Vik Dhillon, Stuart Littlefair, Kendall Ackley, Sergey Belkin, Lisa Kelsey, Tom Killestein, Amit Kumar, Joe Lyman, David O'Neill, Krzysztof Ulaczyk, Ben Godson, Dan Jarvis, Danny Steeghs, Duncan K. Galloway, Paul O'Brien, Gavin Ramsay, Kanthanakorn Noysena, Rubina Kotak, Rene Breton, Laura K. Nuttall, Ben Gompertz, Jorge Casares Velázquez, Don Pollacco
Items.Title: The GOTO telescope control system
Items.Abstract: The Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO) operates a network of robotic, wide-field survey telescopes searching for optical transients to gravitational-wave signals and other astronomical events. Since 2023, the network has comprised two antipodal sites in the Canary Islands and Australia, each hosting two independent robotic mounts.    The GOTO Telescope Control System (G-TeCS) is a custom Python software package that manages all operational aspects of the network; from alert processing and target scheduling to on-site hardware operations and monitoring. The central system consists of an alert monitor, observation database and scheduler, which issues targets to the four nodes. Each telescope operates using a system of independent control daemons, with a pilot master control program to coordinate nightly operations. This architecture, in development since 2015, provides a flexible and robust system that now successfully operates the fully autonomous network.

Items.Authors: Declan O'Neill, Jill Juneau, Peter Orel, Sven Herrmann, Gregory Prigozhin, Eric D. Miller, Steven Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Kevan Donlon, Robert Goeke, Catherine E. Grant, Beverly J. LaMarr, Christopher Leitz, Glenn Morris, Abigail Y. Pan, Tonya L. Peshel, Artem Poliszczuk, Haley R. Stueber, Keith Warner
Items.Title: The high-speed FPGA readout system for the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS)
Items.Abstract: The Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) is a Probe-class mission concept designed to deliver arcsecond spatial resolution, high-sensitivity spectral imaging across the 0.3–10 keV band. The AXIS High-Speed Camera, a joint development effort by MIT and Stanford, includes both the detector and the front-end readout electronics required to meet the mission concept’s demanding performance goals. The telescope’s focal plane detector consists of four 1440x1440 pixel charge-coupled devices (CCDs) developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory, each featuring 16 parallel output channels. The readout utilizes the MCRC readout ASIC followed by waveform digitization and digital signal processing. Here, we present the FPGA-based architecture developed to enable high-speed, parallelized readout of these CCD channels. This design demonstrates the goal readout performance for AXIS (20 frames per second) and provides a framework for future high-throughput X-ray missions.

Items.Authors: Ryuji Suzuki, Yoshiyuki Obuchi, Bungo Ikenoue, Risa Shimizu, Naoatsu Hirata, Masaki Morita, Chihiro Tokoku, Masayuki Hattori, Yoko Tanaka, Koji Omata
Items.Title: The InfraRed Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) for TMT: final design of the IRIS imager
Items.Abstract: IRIS (InfraRed Imaging Spectrograph) is one of the first light instrument for the Thirty Meter Telescope. With the wavefront-corrected light fed by the facility Adaptive Optics system, NFIRAOS, IRIS enables diffraction-limited imaging and integral field spectrograph observation in the wavelength coverage from 0.84 to 2.4 microns. The Imaging mode covers 34 x 34 arcsec^2 field of view with 4 mas sampling using 2 x 2 4K pixel NIR detector mosaic. IRIS is in the final stage of the final design phase. This paper reports an overview of the final design of the IRIS Imager along with some details for key design features, analyses, and prototyping results.

Items.Authors: Risa Shimizu, Yoko Tanaka, Yoshiyuki Obuchi, Ryuji Suzuki
Items.Title: The infrared imaging spectrograph (IRIS) for TMT: STOP analysis for the IRIS Imager
Items.Abstract: Infrared Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), a first-light instrument for the Thirty Meter Telescope, is currently in the final design phase. IRIS provides diffraction-limited imaging and integral field spectroscopic capability in the near-infrared with adaptive optics systems (AO). Since unprecedented high-precision astrometry and high sensitivity observations are unique capabilities of IRIS, stability of star images on the detector under thermal disturbances is critical. IRIS is also required to be ready for observation within 8 days from the start of cooling, meeting both image stability and wavefront error requirements. To assess these thermal-related optical performance criteria, a structural–thermal–optical performance (STOP) analysis was conducted for the IRIS Imager.  STOP analysis indicates that the image stability requirements are met on the 8th day since the start of cooling as well as under the thermal disturbances. It also confirms that the wavefront error originated from cooling.

Items.Authors: Yoko Tanaka, Bungo Ikenoue, Ryuji Suzuki, Fumihiro Uraguchi, Yoshiyuki Obuchi, Masayuki Hattori
Items.Title: The infrared imaging spectrograph (IRIS) for TMT: wavefront error budget
Items.Abstract: The Infrared Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) for the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT), currently in its final design phase, must achieve a wavefront error (WFE) below 40 nm RMS across a 34 x 34 arcsec^2 field of view. To verify compliance, a comprehensive WFE budget allocates requirements to optical design, alignment, fabrication, and thermal effects. The optical design, featuring four off-axis conic mirrors and one spherical mirror, achieves a nominal WFE of 4.6 nm RMS, with assembly simulations predicting 9 nm RMS. Surface figure error—the dominant contributor at 32 nm RMS—has been mitigated via two full-scale prototyping efforts, while thermal deformation was evaluated using finite element analysis. The results demonstrate compliance with a 33% contingency margin.

Items.Authors: Luca Di Fabrizio, Francisco Prada, Adriano Ghedina, Rosario Cosentino, Petri Väisänen, Romano Corradi, Arturo Manchado, Robert Content, Guillermo González de Rivera, Carmen Vélez, Sergio López-Buedo, Álvaro Quintana, Kashif Buland, Juan Antonio Leñero-Bardallo, Ángel Rodríguez-Vázquez, Jacob Classen, Enrique Pérez, M. Ángeles Pérez-García, Antonio García-Rios, Kotaro Moriyama, Pedro Ortega, Sergio Fernández-Acosta, Shiang-Yu Wang, Petri Väisänen, Joel Sánchez-Bermúdez
Items.Title: The La Palma Quantum Interferometer (LPQI): an innovative project in optical intensity interferometry
Items.Abstract: Advances in SPAD sensors, originally for autonomous vehicles, now enable high-precision astronomy. The successful use of a 64×64 SPAD array to observe Betelgeuse has inspired the La Palma Quantum Interferometer (LPQI) project. This collaboration aims to link the largest telescopes in La Palma to create an optical intensity interferometer. By correlating single-photon data, LPQI will achieve a resolution 1000x sharper than the Hubble Space Telescope, allowing unprecedented study of black holes, neutron stars, and cosmic expansion.

Items.Authors: Andrew J. Monson, Roger Angel, Chad Bender, Joel Berkson, Sonja Choi, Warren Foster, Kevin Gilliam, Peter Gray, Chris Kruep, Jason Patrou, William Thompson, Richard Wortley
Items.Title: The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope: System Engineering and Requirements
Items.Abstract: The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope (LFAST) is an array of small, low-cost fiber fed telescopes for astronomical spectroscopy. One of the major goals of LFAST is to reduce the cost of fabrication per photon while still achieving community science goals. A key aspect of LFAST design philosophy is that we can prototype sub-systems rapidly and make iterations before proceeding to large scale replication. In this way, we can use this rapid research and development to help inform the requirements between sub-systems. We also run computer simulations to inform those decisions. We will discuss some of the LFAST requirements and how we track and verify them.

Items.Authors: Zsombor Antal, Christian Schwab, Jacob Pember, Julien Storm, Sonja O. T. Choi, Megan Delamer, Andy Monson, Joel Berkson, Glen Douglass, Michael Weber, Andreas Kelz, Gert Raskin, Julian Stuermer, Samuel Halverson, Chad F. Bender, Martin M. Roth, Roger Angel
Items.Title: The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope: trade-off study of high-resolution spectrometer architectures
Items.Abstract: A combination of large collecting aperture and highly efficient high-resolution spectrometers is required for key cases in exoplanet science. Here, we discuss the design studies for a high-resolution spectroscopic facility for the LFAST telescope, a telescope array overcoming the limitations of single-aperture telescopes by combining a large number of 0.76 m telescopes into one facility with a collecting area comparable to an ELT. Every individual telescope couples light to an optical fiber, which is fed to the proposed spectrometers. The paper investigates design trade-offs between single, very large spectrometers in the visible and the near-IR capable of spectrally analysing the combined fiber output of a large number of telescopes, and multiple smaller spectrometers coupled to sub-arrays of equivalent 10-m, 3-m and individual 0.76-m telescopes.

Items.Authors: Shiang-Yu Wang, Chueh-Yi Chou, Masahiko Kimura, Hsin-Yo Chen, Yin-Chang Chang, Pin-Jie Huang, Niels Tromp, Daan Zaalberg, Dennis Dolkens, Mirka Maresca, Juan Pablo Garcia, Jeff Lynn, Jean-Christophe Barriere, Olivier Corpace, Olivier Absil, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Gert Raskine, Salman Muhammade
Items.Title: The MAIV of the wheel systems in the common foreoptics of the ELT METIS
Items.Abstract: The ELT METIS is the mid-infrared instrument for the ELT providing high contrast imaging and integral field unit (IFU) spectroscopy and normal slit spectroscopy. Inside the common optical path, they are 4 wheels: two in the pupil plane and two in the focal plane. They are included to accommodate the atmospheric dispersion correctors, the field apertures, cold stops, slits, vortex phased masks and the pickoff optics for the L and M band spectrograph (LMS). Among the requirement, the repeatability for the LMS pickoff wheel positioning is particularly tight and a special hinge structure is used to reach the goal. In this paper, we will report on the MAIV process of the wheel and the life time result of the LMS wheel.

Items.Authors: Agustín J. Lapi, M. Gamero, B. Cervantes Vergara, B. Irigoyen Gimenez, B. Roach, P. Alpine, G. Fernandez Moroni, A. Drlica-Wagner, C. Chavez Blanco, F. Chierchie, S. Holland
Items.Title: The MAS-CCD: progress toward space- and ground-based astronomical instruments
Items.Abstract: Radiation hardness is a key requirement for detectors in future space-based astronomical instruments. We present preliminary proton-irradiation results for a 16-channel Multiple Amplifier Sensing CCD, a low-noise silicon imager that uses multiple Skipper-CCD output stages connected in series along the serial register. The sensor was irradiated unbiased at room temperature with 64-MeV protons to a fluence of approximately 1.7×10E9 p/cm2, targeting the region containing the multiple in-line amplifiers. After irradiation, the MAS-CCD Skipper amplifiers continued to demonstrate single-photon counting capability. The average node removal inefficiency across all amplifiers remained below the charge transfer inefficiency reference level of 10E−6, with only a modest increase relative to non-irradiated sensors. These preliminary results indicate that the MAS-CCD architecture is a promising candidate for future astronomical missions operating in L2-like radiation environments.

Items.Authors: Jani Achrén, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Andrea Grazian, Matteo Simioni, Johanna Hartke, Petri Väisänen, Seppo Mattila, Roland Wagner, Eric Gendron, Marco Gullieuszik
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: a dynamic pupil image simulation software for the ELT primary mirror
Items.Abstract: Instruments operating with ELT require accurate pupil models to evaluate throughput and PSF stability. We present a dynamic software that simulates the operational condition, obscuration and reflectivity status of the segmented ELT main mirror, for the purposes of providing realistic and recorded pupil images for optical propagation simulations.

Items.Authors: Sebastian Schäfer, Heiko M. Anwand-Heerwart, Jens-Oliver Dette, Vitalii Kostogryz, Petra Rhode, Khalid Zourganne, Johann Witschel
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: AIV phase of the main support structure, the rotating platform, and the access structure subsystems
Items.Abstract: MICADO has entered the Assembly, Integration and Verification (AIV) phase for all major subsystems following the successful Final Design Review. Here we present the AIV activities for the mechanical subsystems delivered by the Institut für Astrophysik und Geophysik Göttingen: the Instrument Support Structure, the Rotating Platform Assembly, and the Access Structure. These elements form the primary mechanical interfaces between MICADO, its service infrastructure, and the ELT Nasmyth platform. We report first results from procurement, manufacturing readiness, tolerance verification, and early assembly steps, including interface control, alignment concepts, and integration tooling. The paper outlines the planned AIV sequence and the expected transition toward system-level integration.

Items.Authors: Juan Olalla, Jörg-Uwe Pott, Benjamin R. Setterholm, José R. Ramos, Ulf Seemann, Ralph Hofferbert, Norbert Münch, Friedrich Müller, Robert J. Harris, Gabriele Rodeghiero, Santiago Barboza, André Boné, Ralf-Rainer Rohloff, Joshua M. Jost, Moritz H. Lerch, Altay T. Polat, Peter Bizenberger, Vianak Naranjo, María Concepción Cárdenas, Udo Neumann
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: characterization of the flat-field and wavelength calibration unit
Items.Abstract: MICADO is a first-light instrument for the ELT. In this work, we describe the assembly and first test campaign of the Flat-field and wavelength Calibration Unit illumination system. We focus on the performance evaluation of the Argon, Krypton, Neon and Xenon pencil gas lamps (used for wavelength calibration of MICADO), both from spectral and photometric standpoints. Extensive analysis is dedicated to line profile characterization at MICADO resolving power with spectral measurements. We provide flux-calibrated spectra, which will serve as a main input for the definition of calibration procedures during operations. Additionally, we assess other performance metrics such as temporal stability or response to different power supplies.

Items.Authors: Lenard Spallek, Florian Lang, Sriprasanna Srivalli Annadevara, Federico Biondi, Kateryna Kravchenko, Andreas Emslander, Fabio Waldhoer, Julian Ziegleder, Luis Neumeier, Jonas Graf, Hakan Özdemir, Eckhard Sturm, Richard Davies, Michael Krzyzowski, Marcel Bornstein, Ilja Aul, Andreas Blömeke
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: First cooldowns of the MICADO Cryostat and lessons learned
Items.Abstract: The MICADO (Multi-AO Imaging Camera for Deep Observations) instrument is one of the first-light instruments for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Once fully integrated, MICADO will provide multiple imaging modes with unprecedented precision. This will be made possible by adaptive optics systems, various cold subsystems and a 3x3 array of H4RG infrared detectors. All of these components, except for the adaptive optics, are housed in the instrument’s core piece: the MICADO-Cryostat. A continuous LN2 flow cryostat built by CRYOVAC Low Temperature Technologies and the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics. Together with specially designed cryogenic control systems, it can provide thermal stability down to one hundredth of a Kelvin. This paper provides a detailed overview of the initial cooldown of the MICADO cryostat, how it operates and its thermal behaviour with respect to all important interfaces, as well as the challenges that had to be overcome during this period.

Items.Authors: Santiago Barboza, André Boné, Ralf-Rainer Rohloff, Friedrich Müller, Ralph Hofferbert, José R. Ramos, Jörg-Uwe Pott, Jakob Vogler, Norbert Münch, Armin Böhm, Tobias Stadler, Tobias Maurer, Peter Bizenberger, Wolfram Schlossmacher, Helmut Espig, James Mulherin, Christopher A. Hall, Corentin Douchement
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: manufacturing of the relay optics
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the Multi-AO Imaging Camera for Deep Observations, is a first-light instrument for the ELT and will initially operate with a Single-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (SCAO) system. Its Relay Optics (RO) relocates the ELT focal plane to the appropriate position inside the MICADO cryostat for the stand-alone SCAO mode. The RO includes a CFRP optical bench, three flat motorized tip-tilt-piston mirrors (M1, M5, M6), three powered mirrors (M2–M4) up to ~500 mm in diameter, and a CFRP protective cover. The MICADO Calibration Assembly (MCA) and its deployment unit (MDU) are also mounted on the bench. Mirror fabrication and testing in their nominal mounts are complete, and all components and verification tools have been delivered to MPIA. Following a successful FDR in 2022, manufacturing is now finished, and the Assembly, Integration, and Verification phase is progressing at full pace toward Preliminary Acceptance Europe (PAE).

Items.Authors: Michael Hartl, Ric Davies, Norbert Geis, Dirk Kampf, Sebastian Rabien, Josef Schubert, Eckhard Sturm
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: optical design of the MICADO cold optics
Items.Abstract: MICADO is the first light instrument for the ELT. In combination with the multi-conjugate adaptive-optics system MORFEO, MICADO will provide two diffraction limited imaging modes with unvignetted field of views of 19”x19” and 51”x51” as well as a long-slit spectroscopy mode at near-infrared wavelengths ranging from 0.8 µm to 2.4 µm.  Its optical design is based on a classical collimator-camera setup. The system incorporates zoom optics for high-resolution imaging, a long-slit spectrograph optimised for compact objects with a resolution of about 10k, and a pupil imager. Both the imager and the spectrograph utilise a full 3x3 mosaic focal plane of HAWAII-4RG™ detectors.  The presentation will cover the key aspects of the optical design and the performance of the two imaging modes.

Items.Authors: Benjamin R. Setterholm, Jörg-Uwe Pott, José Ramos, Ralph Hofferbert, Norbert Münch, Robert J. Harris, Gabriele Rodeghiero, Friedrich Müller, Santiago Barboza, André Boné, Ralf-Rainer Rohloff, Joshua M. Jost, Juan Olalla Pombo, Moritz H. Lerch, Altay T. Polat, Peter Bizenberger, Vianak Naranjo, Armin Böhm
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: realization of the MICADO calibration assembly
Items.Abstract: MICADO (Multi-AO Imaging CAmera for Deep Observations) is a first-light instrument for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), enabling diffraction-limited imaging (~4–10 mas) and spectroscopy (R ≤ 20,000) at near-infrared wavelengths (0.8–2.4 μm). The MICADO Calibration Assembly (MCA) is deployed to rigorously understand the instrument’s performance over its operational lifespan and to provide a reference for data reduction. The MCA is a collection of three independent units affixed to a common mount at a homologous image plane to that of the ELT. Herein, we describe the final design of the MCA nominal hardware, as-built. We further discuss the results of the the first test campaign of the three individual calibration units.

Items.Authors: Arnaud Sevin, Florian Ferreira, Eric Gendron, Fabrice Vidal, Yann Clénet, Damien Gratadour, Ric Davies
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: real-time monitoring and control for AIT activities
Items.Abstract: MICADO SCAO is currently in its Assembly, Integration and Test (AIT) phase, supported by a dedicated optical bench installed at LIRA and by a standalone real-time computer (RTC) prototype. The hard real-time capabilities are provided by COSMIC, while soft real-time functions rely on the ESO RTC Toolkit. This year, the final RTC hardware was received, assembled, and integrated into the RTC rack. While awaiting the next AIT stages on the MICADO SCAO bench, this final hardware has been configured as a development and integration platform, enabling deployment and validation of the latest RTC Toolkit (v5) using ESO simulators.

Items.Authors: Michael Wegner, Jörg Schlichter
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: redundancy-free implementation of common features between preparation and control software
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the near-infrared Multi-AO Imaging Camera for Deep Observations and designated ELT first-light instrument, will be supported and operated in different observation phases by different kinds of software. Here, several instrument-specific functions need to be available across the systems and take into account the heterogeneous architectures, environments, and teams. In a trade-off against duplicated but independent implementations, we have chosen the redundancy-free solution of a single common library. We present its envisaged features along with a discussion of the pros and cons of the considered design options.

Items.Authors: Joshua M. Jost, Jörg-Uwe Pott, André Boné, Benjamin R. Setterholm, Juan Olalla Pombo
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: simulating the impact of sky de-rotation on the astrometric stability of MICADO
Items.Abstract: MICADO is scheduled to be the first-light instrument for the ELT. This work presents a comprehensive simulation analysis of the impact of de-rotating MICADO on the stability of the effective instrument distortion, the SCAO dichroic-dependent distortion and their combined impact on differential astrometric performance at the sub-microarcsecond level. We quantify how these effects evolve over full 360° rotations, evaluate the fidelity of affine, polynomial and interpolation-based corrections and derive calibration strategies that minimize overhead while maintaining the required astrometric precision. While minor design refinements to some of the components may occur, we assume the final design will be sufficiently similar to preserve the qualitative validity of our results.

Items.Authors: Jörg-Uwe Pott, Joshua M. Jost, Benjamin R. Setterholm, Juan Olalla Pombo, Altay T. Polat, Richard Davies, Elena Valenti, Wolfgang Kausch, Janus D. Brink
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: status of developing calibration strategies for the scientific observing modes
Items.Abstract: MICADO is a first light camera of the ELT. The AO-assisted instrument will deliver large diffraction-limited near-infrared images of ~50” diameter with superb angular resolution of 5-10mas and JWST-like sensitivity. We aim for relative astrometric stability down to 50 µas (or 2e-4) at least. In addition, a long-slit spectrograph disperses the light of compact objects with a spectral resolution R~10k onto the massive focal plane array, consisting of 3x3 Hawaii 4RG detectors.    MICADO science goes from solar system objects over exo-planets and black holes up to galactic evolution at highest redshift. This results in a broad range of calibration requirements. We present our concepts to achieve long-term calibration stability in flat field, distortion, intra-pixel sensitivities, optical train performance. We discuss the interplay of MICADO calibration with telescope flexure and night-time conditions (AO performance). A unique feature is the astrometric calibration unit.

Items.Authors: Andrea Grazian, Fernando Pedichini, Matteo Simioni, Jani Achren, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Luca Cortese, Ric Davies, Marco Gullieuszik, Johanna Hartke, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Roberto Piazzesi, Elisa Portaluri, Stefan Raffetseder, Piero Vaccari, Benedetta Vulcani, Roland Wagner, Anita Zanella
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: the PSF reconstruction software
Items.Abstract: The MICADO instrument for the ESO ELT will provide Adaptive Optics  (AO) diffraction-limited NIR imaging and spectroscopy. A critical  component of MICADO is the Point Spread Function Reconstruction (PSF-R)  Software, which is designed to perform a blind reconstruction of the  PSF for all observations using AO telemetry data only, both with the Single  Conjugate (SCAO) and Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) modes of  MICADO. The SCAO PSF-R Pipeline is currently being completed, and  validation with ERIS at VLT has demonstrated high accuracy:  percent-level on-axis and 5-15% off-axis. Initial scientific  simulations confirm that the software meets the necessary precision for  high-quality analysis, securing its role for MICADO's first light and  future ELT operations.

Items.Authors: Alessandro Coppolecchia, Alessandro Attoli, Eleonora Barbavara, Elia Stefano Battistelli, Paolo de Bernardis, Federico Cacciotti, Giuseppe Carboni, Ettore Carretti, Daniele Ciccalotti, Fabio Columbro, Angelo Cruciani, Giuseppe D'Alessandro, Marco De Petris, Federica Govoni, Giovanni Isopi, Adelaide Ladu, Luca Lamagna, Pasqualino Marongiu, Silvia Masi, Matteo Murgia, Alessandro Navarrini, Alessandro Novelli, Andrea Occhiuzzi, Andrea Orlati, Alessandro Paiella, Giorgio Pettinari, Francesco Piacentini, Mauro Pili, Tonino Pisanu, Sergio Poppi, Luca Schirru, Gian Paolo Vargiu, Sofia Ferazzoli, Giancarlo De Gasperis, Sofia Ferazzoli, Davide Marsala, Giampaolo Pisano, Chiara Volpe
Items.Title: The MISTRAL instrument: a cryogenic W-band lumped elements kinetic inductance detector camera for mm-wave astronomy
Items.Abstract: Mistral is a W-band(77–103GHz)cryogenic camera installed at the Gregorian focus of the 64m Sardinia Radio Telescope.Its 415 element Ti/Al LEKID array operates at 0.2K and, coupled to the SRT through a re–imaging  optical system, enables 12arcsec angular–resolution observations in the W–band and provides a 4arcmin instantaneous field of view.The system enables high–resolution millimeter observations for studies of key astrophysical processes across galactic and extragalactic environments.In this contribution, we present the MISTRAL instrument and discuss selected results from its technical commissioning.Specifically, we describe its cryogenic performance;the results confirm theoretical expectations and in-lab performance, demostrationg the system's capability to cool the focal plane to approximately 0.2K.Notably, this is achieved using 100m helium lines between the pulse tube and the compressor in line with previous characterizations of efficiency degradation as a function of line length

Items.Authors: Kevin Munari, Alessandro Costa, Federico Incardona, Sebastiano Spinello, Emilio Mastriani, Fulvio Gianotti, Ismam Abu, Marcello Lodi, Alessandro Tacchini, Marco De Benedetto, Andrea Mandica
Items.Title: The new ASTRI Mini-Array monitoring system: transition to a stand-alone Java architecture with SCDB-driven configuration
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array is an array of nine dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes that will be deployed at Teide Observatory. In this context, the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system coordinates control, monitoring, data acquisition, and real-time data quality assessment across the array. A fundamental sub-system of SCADA is the Monitoring System, which monitors critical parameters and oversees key components, providing comprehensive oversight of both scientific instrumentation and operational infrastructure. The Monitoring System has undergone a major architectural evolution with its transition from an ACS-embedded component to a stand-alone Java application. The new architecture is also centered on the System Configuration Database (SCDB), which provides unified configuration for all monitoring points, including metadata, sampling policies, and alarm thresholds. Collected data are processed and forwarded to the Alarm and Logging Systems, and the Human Machine Interface.

Items.Authors: Sebastiano Spinello, Alessandro Costa, Federico Incardona, Kevin Munari, Emilio Mastriani, Fulvio Gianotti, Ismam Abu, Marcello Lodi, Alessandro Tacchini, Marco De Benedetto, Andrea Mandica
Items.Title: The new version of the ASTRI Mini-Array alarm system
Items.Abstract: Within the ASTRI Mini-Array SCADA infrastructure, the Alarm System detects, prioritises, and notifies abnormal conditions that may affect the safety and performance of telescopes, auxiliary devices, and ICT infrastructure. In October 2025 it completed its transition from an ACS-embedded component to a stand-alone Java application, improving modularity, deployment, and independence from the ALMA Common Software (ACS) middleware. The new architecture is centred on an Alarm Manager that aggregates alarms from OPC-UA (Open Platform Communications – Unified Architecture) servers, ACS Notification Channels, and ICT subsystems, with configuration data managed in the System Configuration Database (SCDB). RESTful APIs expose configuration, status, and alarm information to the Human Machine Interface (HMI) and higher-level orchestration software.

Items.Authors: John Young, Eugene Seneta, Samantha Thompson, Clark Baker, Martin Fisher, Jan Rinze Peterzon, Tim Naylor, Ian Wellaway, Peter Pedersen, Martin Šulc
Items.Title: The patient observer: designing a robotic control system for a ten-year EPRV survey
Items.Abstract: We present the design of the HARPS3 software system, which enables robotic service mode observing with the refurbished 2.5-m Isaac Newton Telescope and the HARPS3 EPRV spectrograph. We have adopted a clean-sheet design based on a distributed, event-driven architecture. Command-response and publish-subscribe messaging patterns are used to coordinate the actions of software components running on different computers and linked by an Ethernet network. The Observing Control Software (OCS) commands the telescope and instrument control applications to acquire the celestial target, configure the instrument and obtain science exposures. Every component of the control software has a simulation mode, allowing a variety of simulation environments to be configured, ranging from a fully simulated telescope and instrument to alternative subsets of the instrument hardware.

Items.Authors: Jeffrey D. Crane, Solange Ramírez, Alan Uomoto, Daniel Bednarski, Kasey Boggs, Antonio Braulio, David Cruz, Carlos Fermino, Tyson Hare, Julian Garcia, Karim Kaismoune, René Laporte, John Piotrowski, Rafael Ribeiro
Items.Title: The preliminary design of the Giant Magellan Telescope commissioning camera
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) Commissioning Camera (ComCam) is a re-imager designed to evaluate telescope performance in both natural seeing and ground layer adaptive optics modes across a six arcminute field of view. As the first imaging instrument for the GMT, it will provide unique public outreach functions and scientific research opportunities by enabling both narrowband and broadband imaging, with associated photometric measurements, optimized at wavelengths between 360 and 950 nm with additional capability both blueward and redward of this range. With an image scale of 0.06 arcseconds per pixel, ComCam will take full advantage of the GMT’s GLAO-corrected image quality under the best predicted conditions. ComCam is under development in the final design phase with first light expected concurrent with that of the GMT.

Items.Authors: Toshiyuki Mizuki, Justin Hom, Bertrand Mennesson, Ramya Anche, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Vanessa P. Bailey, Koji Kawabata, Mitsuhiko Takeuchi, Motohide Tamura, Naoshi Murakami, John Livingston, Jason J. Wang, Schuyler G. Wolff, Guillermo Gonzalez, Eric Shen, Tsutsumi Nagai, Taichi Uyajma
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph community participation program: calibration strategy for the Mueller matrix using on-sky sources
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraphic Instrument on the Roman Space Telescope has a visible polarimetric mode. Accurate calibration of its polarization response is essential for characterizing debris disks, detecting planetary polarization, and diagnosing polarization aberrations. We will observe two unpolarized standards and two polarized standards with intrinsic polarization angles separated by about 45 degrees. These four stars provide the necessary constraints to solve the Mueller matrix such that the known polarization degrees and angles of the standards are correctly recovered. Standards must be single, bright enough for high S/N without saturating, and sufficiently polarized; visibility and operational constraints also apply. From optical catalogs we identified 72 candidates and began a precursor campaign targeting 21 northern objects. Multi-band HONIR polarimetry on the Kanata 1.5 m telescope measures wavelength dependence and enables Serkowski-law extrapolation to the Roman filters.

Items.Authors: Jingwen Zhang, Sophie Noiret, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Jason Wang, Neil Zimmerman, Eric Shen, Alexis Lau, Elodie Choquet, Taichi Uyajma, Chen Xie, Jessica Gersh-Range, Julien Girard, Vanessa Bailey, John Krist, Kevin Ludwick, Alexis Bidot, Arthur Vigan
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph community participation program: corgisim, a simulation suite for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Coronagraphic Instrument
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will feature a pathfinder Coronagraph Instrument to demonstrate advanced high-contrast imaging from space. Roman Coronagraph could obtain imaging and spectroscopy of Jupiter analogs in reflected visible light for the first time. We present the work of developing an open-source simulation package “corgisim” as part of the Roman Coronagraph Community Participate Program. Built on established optical propagation libraries such as PROPER and CGISim, corgisim provides a publicly available Python framework for end-to-end simulations of Roman-CGI observations. The package produces high-fidelity, format-compliant data for pre-launch calibration, pipeline testing, and community applications such as target planning and selection and observation planning. We will give an overview of corgisim’s infrastructure, and current implementation across planned imaging, polarimetry, and spectroscopy modes. We will also provide guidance on how users can employ the software.

Items.Authors: Amanda Chavez, Jason Wang, Vanessa Bailey, Maxwell Millar-Blanchaer, Julien H. Girard, Sergi Hildebrandt, John Krist, Julia Milton, Marie Ygouf
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: data reduction pipeline astrometric calibration
Items.Abstract: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program has led the development of a python-based, open source data reduction pipeline (corgidrp) to quantify the performance of the Roman Space Telescope coronagraph instrument and to process its data products. Here, we present the astrometric calibration function within the greater data reduction pipeline, outline the methods for computing critical astrometric calibration measurements, and contextualize this calibration process within corgidrp. Additionally, we discuss the results of end-to-end testing and show that all formal Technology Demonstration Threshold Requirements for this calibration step are satisfied.

Items.Authors: Ramya M. Anche, Toshiyuki Mizuki, Vanessa P. Bailey, Eric J. Cady, Clarissa Do Ó, Jessica A. Gersh-Range, Justin Hom, Alexis Lau, John Livingston, Bertrand Mennesson, Maxwell A. Millar-Blanchaer, Julia Milton, Naoshi Murakami, Tsutsumi Nagai, Sophie Noiret, Eric Shen, Motohide Tamura, Taichi Uyajma, Jason J. Wang, Schuyler G. Wolff, Cynthia Wong, Chen Xie, Marie Ygouf, Jingwen Zhang, Julien H. Girard
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: simulation of on-sky polarimetric observations, data reduction, and analysis
Items.Abstract: Reflected-light polarimetry of an exoplanet helps constrain and break degeneracies in atmospheric properties, and polarized light observations of debris disks enable exploration of the disk’s dust-grain properties. The best-effort polarimetric mode of the Roman Coronagraph Instrument will be able to perform multi-wavelength observations of planetary systems using the Hybrid Lyot Coronagraph (HLC) and the Shaped Pupil Coronagraph (SPC). In this paper, we demonstrate the capabilities of the polarimetric mode of the Roman Coronagraph for targets chosen in the nominal observing plan. We simulate science target observations and calibration products using the corgisim package and perform data reduction and analysis using the corgidrp, incorporating all noise factors and instrumental polarization effects from modeled Mueller matrices. The final retrieved polarization fraction (p) indicates that the polarimetry mode of the Roman Coronagraph Instrument meets the goal uncertainty of ~ 3%.

Items.Authors: Dmitry Savransky, Rifah Tasnim, Saanika Choudhary, Hovik Grigoryan, Justin Hom, Bijan Nemati, Neil Zimmerman, Ramya Anche, Nicholas Phillips, Louie Donesa, Parth Mittal, Amira Razack, Savaas Iqbal, Javier Majumdar, Schuyler G. Wolff, Vanessa P. Bailey
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: target database and tools
Items.Abstract: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument will, for the first time, demonstrate high-contrast imaging with active wavefront control in visible wavelengths from space. In preparation for the Coronagraph’s commissioning and observing programs, the Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program has developed a target database and associated ecosystem of publicly accessible tools for observation planning and scheduling. The target database includes planet and disk hosts, calibration stars, reference stars, and engineering program targets. The database is designed to operate in conjunction with a variety of tools, including an exposure time calculator, a pointing and keepout calculator, and a reference star selection tool. We describe the current schema and contents of the database and demonstrate how it and its associated tools are being used for observation planning.

Items.Authors: Arthur Vigan, Alexis Bidot, Vincent Chambouleyron, Garreth Ruane, Laurent Pueyo, Mamadou N'Diaye, Kjetil Dohlen
Items.Title: The Roman Coronagraph Community Participation Program: using the Zernike wavefront sensor for a full characterisation of the Roman Space Telescope and the Coronagraph Instrument
Items.Abstract: The Roman Space Telescope Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) will demonstrate a series of technologies and techniques to enable the direct detection of reflected-light planets with space-based observatories. Among the several available observing modes and coronagraphic devices embarked in CGI, there is a transmissive Zernike wavefront sensor (ZWFS) that can be used to directly measure optical aberrations in the system. In this work, we advocate for the commissioning of this unique observing mode. We investigate the sensitivity of the ZWFS and demonstrate how it can be used for a full observatory characterisation. We use the CGI simulator and other tools developed and supported by the Roman community participation program (CPP). This type of analysis is crucial for understanding the stability of the Roman observatory and to prepare the path towards HWO.
